# Tobit Chapter 8 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 8 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_008_page_001.jpg

---

**1** When they had finished eating, they brought Tobias in to her.

**2** As he went, he remembered the words of Raphael. He took the ashes of the incense and laid upon them the heart and liver of the fish, and made smoke with them.

**3** The demon smelled it and fled to the upper parts of Egypt, and Raphael went and bound him there, shackled forever.

**4** When they were shut in together, Tobias rose from the bed and said to her, "Rise up, my sister, and let us pray that the Lord will have mercy upon us."

**5** Tobias began and said: "Blessed are you, O God of our fathers, and blessed is your name throughout all the ages of ages. Let the heavens bless you, and all your creation, throughout all the ages.

**6** You made Adam and gave him Eve his wife as helper and support; from both of them came the seed of all mankind. You yourself said, 'It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.'

**7** And now, O Lord, it is not out of lust that I take this my sister, but in truth. Command that mercy be shown to me and to her, and that we may come to old age together."

**8** They both said together, "Amen, amen."

**9** They slept through the night. Raguel rose and went out and dug a grave,

**10** saying, "Perhaps he will die as well." And Raguel went back into his house

**11** and said to his wife Edna, "Send one of the maidservants to look and see whether he is alive; and if he is not, we will bury him before anyone finds out."

**12** The maidservant opened the door and went in and found them both asleep.

**13** She came out and told them that he was alive.

**14** Then Raguel blessed God, saying: "Blessed are you, O God, with every pure and holy blessing. Let your holy ones bless you, and all your creatures, and all your angels, and all your chosen ones bless you forever.

**15** Blessed are you, because you have made me glad, and what I feared has not come to pass. Rather, you have dealt with us according to your great mercy.

**16** Blessed are you, because you have had mercy on these two only children. Show them mercy, O Master. Grant them health in life, joy, mercy, and gladness.

**17** Grant them, O Lord, long life in gladness."

**18** Then he commanded his servants to fill in the grave before daylight.

**19** He told his wife to bake many loaves of bread, and he himself went to the herd and brought two oxen and four rams and commanded them to be prepared. And they began their preparations.

**20** He called Tobias and swore to him, saying, "You shall not leave here for fourteen days,

**21** but shall stay here eating and drinking with me, and shall gladden the heart of my daughter who has been deeply afflicted. Take half of all that I possess and return in peace to your father; the other half will come to you when my wife and I have died. Take heart, my child. I am your father, and Edna is your mother, and we belong to you and to your sister, now and forever. Take heart, child."

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

Chapter 8 balances two registers: the numinous (the exorcism, the prayer) and the domestic (Raguel's anxious grave-digging, the feast preparations). LOGOS aims to honor both without collapsing either into the other.

- **Verses 2-3**: The exorcism is treated with spare directness. "Made smoke with them" is a formal rendering of the causative; no expansion is needed. "Shackled forever" captures the Greek desmios eis tous aionas.
- **Verse 7**: "In truth" (ep' aletheias) versus "out of lust" (ep' porneias) — the contrast is preserved as the moral center of the prayer. LOGOS avoids "fornication" as archaic and "sexual desire" as too clinical; "lust" retains the pejorative force intended.
- **Verse 9**: Raguel's grave-digging is rendered with understated irony: "he rose and went out and dug a grave" with no commentary. The text speaks for itself.
- **Verse 11**: "Before anyone finds out" — a natural rendering of the Greek mede gnoi tis; LOGOS keeps the social anxiety present.
- **Verse 14**: Raguel's blessing is structured as a doxology; LOGOS maintains the parallel "blessed are you" anaphora.
- **Verse 21**: The inheritance terms are rendered with legal precision. "Belong to you" for the relationship language captures the family-adoption dynamic of the scene.

*— LOGOS*
